subject: Help please: how to specify a hierarchical prior

messages.author: af10d02419f93739
messages.subject: Help please: how to specify a hierarchical prior
parts:
Dear All, 
  I am trying to learn INLA by fitting a very simple hierarchical model: 


Y ~ N(theta, 1/lambda^2) ## so that lamda^2 is the precision 
theta | lambda^2 ~ N(mu, 1/(m * lambda^2) ## This is like a prior made up of m observations 
lambda^2 ~ Gamma(a, b) 

There is no random effect. 
A ton of thanks to anyone who would care to help by suggesting how to code. 

Best wishes, Sujit

messages.author: 334c7505e0b5cf65
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Help please: how to specify a hierarchical prior
parts:
> Y ~ N(theta, 1/lambda^2) ## so that lamda^2 is the precision
> theta | lambda^2 ~ N(mu, 1/(m * lambda^2) ## This is like a prior made up of m observations
> lambda^2 ~ Gamma(a, b)

I do not think that you can fit this model with INLA because lambda^2 also appears in the prior of theta, i.e., hyper parameters of the likelihood cannot appear in any other parts of the model. Perhaps there is a workaround using a reparameterization of the model, some of the INLA advanced features or sampling [1].

Best,

Virgilio

[1] https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-newmodels.html

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Help please: how to specify a hierarchical prior
parts:
Hi Sujit,

as Virgilio says, it's not immediately obvious how to fit this model,
but there is a reparameterisation trick that can work for models like
this:

First, define a model as
theta ~ N(0, \infty)
(y_i | theta, lambda) ~ N(theta, 1/lambda^2)
Then, introduce a dummy observation that links theta to its desired prior:
(z | theta, lambda) ~ N(sqrt(m)*theta, 1/lambda^2)
where the dummy observation is set to
z = -sqrt(m)*mu
Since both y_i and z have the same observation noise, the
z-"observation" can simply be added to the observation vector, and a
weight sqrt(m) used for that observation in the predictor (can be
setup with inla.stack(), but I think one can also rescale the variance
for that observation, as a shorter alternative).

If the y-observations weren't there, that would lead to
(theta|z,lambda) ~ N(mu, 1/lambda^2)
as desired, since it's equivalent to
theta = mu + e
where
e ~ N(0,1/m/lambda^2)

Equivalently, theta ~ N(mu,\infty), z = 0, would give the same result.

To set this up practically, I think you need
f(theta, model ="iid",
hyper=list(prec=list(fixed=TRUE,initial=SomeSmallValue))))
where SomeSmallValue is sufficiently small but positive approximation
of 1/\infty.

There are several variations for how to implement this trick.

Finn
